tagline: Old trail routes link mill country, pine forest and Gray.
intro: The Ocmulgee-Piedmont Scenic Byway connects the Ocmulgee River with Gray by way of pine forest and small communities. Georgia DOT includes it among the state’s designated scenic byways, highlighting Jones County history, the Piedmont National Wildlife Refuge and East Juliette’s mill village. The wooded stretch follows Round Oak-Juliette Road; the other leg uses State Route 11. The refuge’s ridges carry loblolly pines, with hardwoods along creek bottoms and in upland coves. Streams and beaver ponds add wetland habitat to the forest.

Both roads follow earlier Native American trails. The SR 11 corridor became a major route between Hillsboro and Clinton, Jones County’s nineteenth-century seat. Opposing forces fought along it at Sunshine Church in 1864; later that year Sherman followed the route through the county on his March to the Sea. The forested leg also crosses land with a changed purpose: the refuge was established in 1939 to demonstrate wildlife restoration on eroded land.

Drive from the river end, with Juliette on the west bank and the mill village across the Ocmulgee. Head east through the refuge to Round Oak, then south on SR 11 through Wayside and Bradley to downtown Gray’s depot. GDOT describes the two legs as approximately twelve and nine miles respectively.

moments.title: Juliette
moments.text: Juliette’s main street changed roles after the filming of Fried Green Tomatoes. The film sets were renovated into a tourist district, including a working Whistle Stop Cafe. The community itself formed from the merger of Brownsville and Iceberg and took the name of Juliette McCracken, a railroad engineer’s daughter. It occupies the Ocmulgee’s west bank, across from East Juliette’s mill village. Round Oak-Juliette Road crosses the river here and continues east to Round Oak. The Ocmulgee also marks the county boundary here, separating Monroe County on Juliette’s side from Jones County across the water.

moments.title: Piedmont National Wildlife Refuge
moments.text: Loblolly pines occupy the ridges at Piedmont, while hardwoods grow along creek bottoms and in upland coves. This forest grew back on exhausted farmland. Repeated cotton planting caused erosion and depleted the soil; by the 1930s, lost topsoil had exposed red clay. Established in 1939, the refuge was intended to demonstrate that wildlife could return to eroded land. The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service now uses prescribed fire, thinning and regeneration to maintain habitat. Streams and beaver ponds provide wetlands for migrating waterfowl. The refuge covers 35,000 acres and serves as a model for managing forest for wildlife.
moments.notice: Pines occupy ridges; hardwoods follow creek bottoms and grow in scattered upland coves.

moments.title: Round Oak
moments.text: Round Oak began as Sylvania in 1807, then took a name honoring an ancient oak used as a Native American gathering place. A depot built in 1885 brought an economic upswing that lasted into the early 1920s. Sunshine Church carries another part of the local story: Sherman’s forces burned it in 1864, and it was rebuilt at Round Oak in 1875. The community sits on SR 11, north-northwest of Gray.
